EU AUDIT approval in Nov 2026 : This could be the first sign of a meaningful rate of change in the business, but investors need to understand that the recovery will take time.

Even after a positive EU audit, the company will have to go through individual regulatory approvals and obtain product registrations market by market. 
Only after these approvals come through can it meaningfully start ramping up operations. 

Management has indicated that reaching meaningful scale at Ambernath could take another 1–1.5 years after a positive audit outcome.

However, let's not forget what this development potentially solves : the Ambernath issue, which is currently creating approximately 6 % EBITDA margin pressure.

The next important milestone will be revenue ramp-up at the facility. Management has indicated that annual revenue of approximately Rs 160–200 crore would be the sweet spot for Ambernath to achieve break-even.

Until the facility reaches this level, it will continue to carry an operating cost burden. Beyond that, the operating leverage story should gradually start playing out, with incremental revenue translating into better profitability. 

But there is another factor that needs equally close monitoring: LATAM markets.

Regulatory hurdles in markets such as Colombia, Peru and Uruguay have disrupted sales of certain high-margin products. Customers now require additional import authorisations, which could take several months. (Q4FY27 will be key to watch..) 

This is important because the disruption is not just affecting revenue but also the company's product and geographical mix, thereby putting pressure on margins.

Management expects further developments as the regulatory situation evolves. We should closely track customer authorisations, restoration of orders and the recovery of high-margin sales.

The third factor is raw material and solvent inflation, which has also contributed to margin pressure. The extent to which the company can pass on these increased costs will be another important variable.

Personal thoughts : The larger investment thought

There are essentially three factors currently weighing on Supriya Lifescience's profitability:

1. Ambernath: Regulatory approvals, product registrations and eventual revenue ramp-up.

2. LATAM: Resolution of regulatory hurdles and restoration of high-margin sales.

3. Raw material costs: Normalisation of input costs and recovery of pricing margins.

The important thing is that these factors have different timelines and need to be tracked independently.

With the stock price already reflecting significant pessimism, this is a good time to study the business closely and track the rate of change across these operating parameters.

The objective is not to predict an immediate turnaround but to identify early signs of improvement before they become fully visible in reported earnings.

Keep tracking the regulatory milestones, revenue ramp-up, capacity utilisation, EBITDA break-even and margin recovery.

If these developments start falling into place, the operating leverage story could become an important earnings driver over the coming years.

This is an exercise in tracking the rate of change, not merely tracking quarterly numbers. 
The opportunity, if it materialises, will be in identifying the inflection in fundamentals ahead of the broader market.

Finished reading @SoniaGandhi ji’s memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, last night.

Couldn’t stop once I had started.  It is riveting, deeply moving, and quietly shattering.

I am overwhelmed not only by her remarkable life, but by her candour, her nerves of steel, her sensitivity, and her ability to hold her head high in the face of cruel adversities. 

But above all, I am moved by her faith in love - the love that made her cross continents, love that nurtured her, the love she feels for India, the love that makes her belong. 

The love that was crushed before her eyes, yet the same love that has sustained her, and kept her going - again and again - and is the bedrock of everything she has done and continues to do.

What left me truly spellbound, though, is her sense of duty and responsibility.

I have admired her my entire life, but reading this book has deepened that respect into something I can’t explain in words. 

Despite unimaginable violence and irreparable losses, she never allowed herself to become bitter. Her capacity to forgive even those who destroyed her world - left me in awe. 

She is fully aware of the vicious lies her opponents have spread about her for decades. And she addresses each one with her trademark simplicity and dignity.

An intensely private person has finally chosen to tell her story on her own terms. For the first time, she speaks of battling cancer not once but twice. For the first time one gets to know that before her two children, she bore the pain of losing her firstborn. 

I wept as I read - a lot actually. It is almost unbearable to imagine the pain inflicted upon her, yet not once did she ever play victim.

She is deeply admired - for her courage, her grace, and the quiet strength with which she has carried so much. But the book will make many people understand her and love her - even more.

‘Belonging’ is not merely a memoir. It is a testament to a life lived with love as both compass and anchor, and to a woman who refused to let grief harden her heart. Some stories do not just move you, they stay with you, reminding you what true resilience looks like. This is one of them. 

At its heart, ‘Belonging’ is one of the greatest love stories of our time!

Why is Supriya Lifescience falling? 📉
The stock fell from ₹870 to ₹631 in three sessions, a 27% drop. It's now 40% below its June peak of ₹1,052.
The trigger wasn't revenue, it was margins.
Q2 FY27:
• Revenue ₹206 cr, up 3% YoY
• EBITDA ₹45 cr, down 38%
• Margin 22%, compared with 35%+ last year
• Profit ₹29 cr, down 42%
"The big hit: margin guidance cut"

FY27 EBITDA margin guidance was cut from 33–35% to 23–25%. In August, management had kept 33–35%, even though Q1 margin had already fallen to 25%.

Three reasons, roughly 10–12 points of margin lost:
1️⃣ Ambernath plant: about ₹60 cr of FY27 costs with almost no revenue. The EU audit has moved to November.
2️⃣ LATAM: high-margin products were reclassified as controlled substances in Colombia, Peru and Uruguay. Customers now need import permits, which take 4–5 months. Orders aren't lost, but they're delayed.
3️⃣ Raw materials and solvents: costs are up. Price increases have been passed on, but they'll take 2–3 quarters to show.

What's still intact:
• FY27 revenue target of ₹1,000 cr is maintained. That needs about ₹604 cr in H2.
• Pipeline: anaesthetic CMO deal close to signing, ADHD intermediates, contrast media launch next quarter, a cardiovascular intermediate, and whey protein.
• Ambernath could eventually do ₹450–500 cr of revenue. Breakeven is about ₹160–200 cr.
What's missing: no FY28 margin guidance. Ambernath needs 1–1.5 years after approval to scale, so don't assume margins snap back to 33–35%.

I went through 13 Q2 earnings calls of some companies focusing on what management expects over the next 6–12 months.

One thing stood out: Most companies raised or maintained guidance, but the numbers tell a slightly different story.

GNG Electronics: Revenue growth raised to 40%, partly benefiting from rising new-laptop prices.

CP Plus: Revenue guidance raised, but maintaining 14–15% EBITDA margins implies H2 margins of 13%.

Syrma SGS: Growth guidance raised to 40–45%, but margin guidance cut to 10–10.5%.

Lupin: US sales guidance implies a significant slowdown in H2. FY28 could be a consolidation year.

Muthoot Microfin: Profit target intact, but H2 needs a stronger quarterly run-rate.

Jyoti CNC: Achieving margin guidance depends partly on French export licences.

Azad Engineering: Growth intact, but the revenue ramp has shifted towards Q4.

Sansera: Higher capex, but implied H2 revenue is broadly flat versus H1.

Sansera Engineering Q2 FY27: Precision beyond auto, with a bigger investment cycle ahead

Sansera's diversification is becoming visible in the factory and the numbers. The same engineering base that supplies connecting rods and crankshafts is expanding into aircraft components and precision parts for semiconductor-manufacturing equipment.

The interesting development is that these newer businesses are growing while the automotive business is also expanding. Sansera is broadening what it can manufacture, increasing the complexity of its parts and investing ahead of customer programmes.

Q2 consolidated performance:
• Revenue: ₹1,091.45cr, up 32.3% YoY.
• EBITDA excluding other income: ₹211.23cr, up 47.6%.
• EBITDA margin: 19.4%, versus 17.3% a year ago.
• Group PAT: ₹108.65cr, up 52.2%.

1. The mix is changing without the core shrinking

Auto ICE product sales grew 18.2%, even as their share of product sales fell from 72.9% to 65.7% YoY. Non-auto's share increased from 13.2% to 20.9%.

These mix figures exclude scrap and other operating income. They describe the composition of product sales, rather than percentages calculated from consolidated revenue.

Passenger-vehicle product sales grew 42.4%. Tech-agnostic and xEV product sales together grew 27%. Premium vehicles, more engineered content per vehicle and OEMs buying more components from specialist suppliers are expanding Sansera's opportunities beyond simply following vehicle volumes.

One concrete development: management reported a pilot order linked to a two-wheeler OEM's move from in-house production to outsourcing. Successful execution must come before a much larger programme can be assumed.

Geography also needs care. Some new orders from global vehicle manufacturers relate to engine programmes being built in India. An international customer relationship can therefore generate domestic business.

2. Two order books, with very different meanings

At September-end, Sansera reported:

• ADS: ₹5,869.7cr of cumulative unexecuted backlog across approximately five years. ADS covers aerospace, defence and semiconductor equipment.
• Non-ADS: ₹2,241cr of estimated peak annual revenue from new business, expected to reach that peak within roughly three years.

The second number is a future annual sales level from awarded programmes, not a cumulative amount waiting to be shipped. Adding the two would produce a misleading order-book headline.

There is another important comparison. In the August call, management had already disclosed an ADS backlog of roughly ₹5,750cr after a large semiconductor-equipment order received after June-end. Much of the increase from June to September was therefore already known.

The more useful development is how that work moves through equipment installation, customer validation and production ramp-up.

In the previous call, ADS head Hari Krishnan explained the constraint:
“the significant or the defining lead time is the arrival of the mother machine.”

The specialised production equipment has to arrive before meaningful volumes can follow. In August, management expected significant revenue from that large semiconductor order in calendar 2027, with a peak in calendar 2029. A five-year order does not become next year's revenue simply because it is booked.

3. Semiconductor capability is advancing, but concentration remains

Q2 ADS revenue was ₹164.3cr, taking H1 to ₹309.7cr. These figures include the business's scrap and tooling income.

Management described validations for more complex semiconductor-equipment components and efforts to move further into assemblies. These are valuable steps: supplying a larger, more complicated package can increase the work captured from each customer.

Demand is linked to semiconductor-equipment investment, which in turn benefits from AI infrastructure and chip-capacity spending. Customer investment cycles and equipment-delivery schedules remain relevant risks.

The current semiconductor business still depends on one customer. Management hopes to add a second during Q3; it has not announced that conversion as completed.

On exclusivity, management was explicit:
“I don’t think we’ll be single source.”

Customers are developing multiple suppliers, including in India. Precision capability and successful validation help Sansera compete for more work, but they do not create an assured monopoly over those parts.

Aerospace progress also has different stages. The company reported its first Safran business in the quarter. Separately, the engine-blisk development remains under validation. The latter is not yet a proven commercial revenue stream, and potential investment for that opportunity is excluded from the current capex plan.

4. The larger capex plan changes the scale of execution

FY27 planned capex has increased from approximately ₹500cr to ₹800cr, with about half directed towards ADS. Management says some newer programmes are moving faster than typical automotive projects, requiring investment sooner.

The presentation indicates incremental asset turns of 2.0–2.2 times for ADS versus 1.25–1.3 times for automotive. That suggests more annual revenue per rupee of assets once production matures. It does not remove the time needed for commissioning, approvals and utilisation to build.

Near-term milestones include:
• The expanded ADS bay becoming fully operational during Q3 FY27.
• The dedicated defence facility starting around late Q3 or early Q4.
• Sansera–Nichidai beginning production or sample production towards the end of Q4, with customer conversion still to follow.

The defence facility initially relocates existing machines and gives the business dedicated attention. Proposed sheet-metal capabilities and larger orders are still developing.

The Nichidai venture targets steering, driveline and related precision components. Discussions around humanoid components are interesting, but the company has not provided a firm commercial revenue forecast for them.

5. Better margins do not make the investment cash-free

H1 statutory operating cash flow was ₹222.31cr, ahead of reported group PAT of ₹196.01cr.

However, cash paid for property, plant, equipment and intangibles was ₹356.86cr, with another ₹30.01cr invested in the Nichidai joint venture. Growth investment exceeded operating cash generation.

Inventory absorbed about ₹226cr, partly offset by higher supplier payables. Company-reported net debt increased from about ₹60cr in March to ₹261cr in September. Interest costs are already rising, and management expects some further increase as the business expands.

Margin quality also needs a careful reading. Q2 included a ₹16.7cr minimum-wage provision, with a catch-up from around mid-May. The higher wage base is recurring even though part of this quarter's expense relates to earlier months. Adding back the entire amount permanently would overstate sustainable profitability.

Richer business mix and operating leverage have absorbed some input, freight and labour pressure. Customer compensation for certain cost increases is still being pursued, so it should not be counted before it is secured.

6. The outlook is stronger, but avoid extrapolating the first half

The closing Q&A put FY27 revenue at ₹4,250–4,300cr. Against FY26 revenue of about ₹3,498cr, that implies roughly 21.5–22.9% growth, above the earlier high-teens-to-20% discussion.

After H1 revenue of ₹2,112.7cr, the range implies H2 revenue of approximately ₹2,137–2,187cr. That is only about 1–4% above H1, rather than another dramatic sequential step-up. Management made the outlook conditional on post-festive demand and geopolitical developments.

The presentation retains ADS revenue guidance of ₹550–600cr for FY27. Despite a stronger current run rate, a higher formal annual target has not been published.

Longer term, management aspires to ADS contributing 35–40% of revenue around the end of the decade. A refreshed strategy and firmer targets are expected towards the financial year-end. Capacity potential, aspirational mix and contracted revenue should remain separate in any forecast.

Kyro Read

Sansera is demonstrating that its precision-engineering skills can serve larger markets while its automotive foundation continues to grow.

The investment case now depends on converting qualified components and customer programmes into sustained production, while spreading semiconductor exposure across more customers and earning adequate returns on the higher capital deployed.

Customer approvals, commissioning progress, inventory requirements and the distinction between awarded work and early development will explain the next phase better than one large combined “order book” number.

SANSERA ENGINEERING | Q2 & H1 Concall Updates: 

The story is Sansera’s transition from an automotive-focused precision engineering company towards a larger Aerospace & Defence (ADS) business.

1.
Q2 revenue 1,091.5 Cr (+32% YoY)
EBITDA 211.2 Cr (+48%); margin 19.4%, up ~200 bps.
PAT 108.6 Cr (+52%).
H1 revenue ₹2,112.7 Cr (+33%); EBITDA 407.3 Cr (+48%).
H1 reported PAT 196 Cr; 208.7 Cr excluding the Q1 litigation settlement impact.
Gross margin expanded 180 bps to 43%. However, employee costs, other expenses and depreciation also increased. Mgmt expects a steady margin profile.

2. Automotive: strong core business
Q2 automotive revenue was 669.7 Cr (+18%), around 65% of revenue. PV, two-wheelers, tech-agnostic automotive and XCV delivered their best-ever qtrs.

Automotive new-business order book reached 2,241 Cr of peak annual revenue potential, broadly equally split between domestic and exports. New wins include a tractor customer, PV engine programmes and a pilot outsourcing order from a two-wheeler OEM.

3. ADS: the key strategic growth engine

Q2 ADS revenue: 164.3 Cr; H1: 309.7 Cr.

ADS order backlog: 5,870 Cr versus 4,440 Cr in the previous quarter, executable over five years.💡

Mgmt 👉this is a rolling order book, with fresh wins adding to future execution.
ADS currently contributes ~15% of revenue. Mgmt’s ambition is to take this to 35–40% by decade-end.

4. Aerospace, semiconductors and defence

Aerospace: Two new customers added; first Safran engine-component business won in Q2. Rolls-Royce development has achieved agreed milestones, but validation is awaited; possible conclusion in Q3 FY27.

Semiconductors: Most of the top 10 complex parts for the existing customer have been validated. Mgmt hopes to add a second customer in Q3 FY27 and move towards assembly. Customers use multiple suppliers; exclusivity should not be assumed.
Defence: Dedicated facility expected by end-Q3/early-Q4 FY27. A couple of sizeable opportunities are in final stages. Additional 15–20 Cr capex may be needed if these wins materialise.

5. Capex: 
FY27 capex increased from 500 Cr to 800 Cr, with ~400 Cr earmarked for ADS.
Potential revenue capacities indicated :

Expanded ADS facility: ~1,500 Cr.
New facility: ~1,000–1,500 Cr.

Defence facility: ~400–500 Cr.

( Overall 👉Almost 2X kind of FY26 rev.)

The expanded bay is expected to be operational in Q3; the defence facility by end-Q3/early-Q4; the new facility towards the end of next calendar year.

6. New opportunities
Nichidai JV: Three forging press lines planned initially. Sample/commercial production expected towards end-Q4 FY27; customer discussions are underway.

Humanoid robotics: Developing complex aluminium forged and machined components for a North American customer. Still at development stage; no confirmed order or revenue potential disclosed.

Sheet-metal forming is being considered to address larger defence and aerospace packages.

7. Other updates:
Sweden operates at ~80–85% efficiency. Focus is on automation and engineering improvements, with a 10–12% return target; no major expansion planned.
US plant plans are being reconsidered amid customer delays and tariff uncertainty. Mgmt currently prefers sourcing from India.

MMRFIC is an associate, not a subsidiary. Sansera’s holding is ~47% after full CCPS conversion. Its activities include anti-drone and electronic-warfare radars; it is excluded from Sansera’s capex and revenue projections.

Acquisitions/JVs remain under evaluation, subject to strategic fit.

8. Guidance 🎯
FY27 revenue indication: 4,250–4,300 Cr. Healthy H2, subject to industry demand and geopolitical developments.

FY30 revenue aspiration is 8,000 Cr 💡

A new five-year vision statement is expected by end-FY27.

Overall : Strong call with clear growth focus and future growth oriented, now execution will be key, the order book and investments must reflect in stongvbottom line and cash flows.

A Question I Received from an Investor: 
What Exactly Went Wrong with Supriya Lifesciences' LATAM Business, How Much Revenue Was Impacted, and What Should We Watch Going Forward?

Supriya Lifesciences hit a 20% lower circuit following its Q2 FY27 results. The stock subsequently corrected another 7% on Muhurat trading and another 6–7% thereafter...

While the sharp decline in profitability has understandably disappointed investors, I think we need to look beyond the headline numbers and understand what actually happened to the business.

This post will  focus on the LATAM disruption, because it has implications for both revenue growth and the company's historically attractive EBITDA margins.

What exactly happened?
During the Q2 earnings call, management explained that regulatory changes in three LATAM markets – Colombia, Peru and Uruguay – resulted in certain products being reclassified as controlled substances.

Earlier, customers could import these products relatively freely. Following the changes, customers now require additional import authorizations before shipments can resume.

Management indicated that existing customer purchase orders and demand visibility were available, but customers now need to obtain fresh import authorizations. The process could take approximately 4–5 months.

Consequently, some higher-margin regulated-market sales were deferred. Management also indicated that the entire lost LATAM contribution may not return within FY27.

The important distinction is that management describes this as a regulatory and timing disruption rather than a complete loss of underlying demand.

However, purchase orders are not guaranteed future sales. We will need to see actual shipment recovery.

What did we find on the regulatory changes and affected products?
I tried to cross-check the regulatory developments in all three countries against Supriya's published product portfolio.

In Uruguay, Decree 198/025, dated September 2025, updated the country's controlled-substance framework. The updated national register includes substances such as Esketamine, Ketamine and Dexmedetomidine. These are relevant portfolio overlaps because Supriya has products in these categories.

However, the consolidated register does not establish that all these molecules were newly added through this particular decree or that they were responsible for Supriya's lost orders.

In Colombia, Resolution 116 of 2026 updated the national lists of controlled narcotics, psychotropic substances, precursors and controlled medicines. One important point is that newly controlled precursors should not automatically be confused with finished pharmaceutical products. I could not establish a direct link between every newly controlled substance and Supriya's existing commercial sales.

In Peru, the Ministry of Health published Resolution 831-2026/MINSA in September 2026, proposing updates to controlled-substance lists. Ketamine is an important potential overlap with Supriya's portfolio. However, this document was a proposal for consultation, not confirmation that a new import restriction had already become effective.

My interpretation is that there appears to be a broader regulatory tightening and updating of controlled-substance frameworks across these markets.

But we should not assume that every molecule appearing in the updated lists was newly controlled or contributed to Supriya's lost revenue.

The exact product-country mapping has not been disclosed by management. Esketamine and Ketamine are portfolio overlaps worth investigating, not confirmed explanations of the Q2 sales disruption.

How significant was LATAM historically?
This is where the situation becomes interesting.

LATAM had become an increasingly important geographical market for Supriya.

Its contribution to export revenue, as disclosed in historical company commentary, was approximately 11% in FY24, increased to 22% in FY25, remained around 20% in FY26 and Q1 FY27, before falling to approximately 12% in Q2 FY27.

The company had therefore built a meaningful business in these markets over the years.

The fall from approximately 20% to 12% in Q2 is significant, especially because these were higher-realization and higher-margin products.

In other words, the issue is not simply lower sales. It is the loss of a favourable revenue mix.

How much revenue could have been impacted?
Let's do our own indicative calculation.

Q2 FY27 revenue was approximately Rs 206.3 crore, with exports contributing around 80%.

This implies export revenue of approximately Rs 165 crore.

Assuming LATAM represented approximately 20% of exports under normal conditions, compared with the reported 12% contribution in Q2, the estimated quarterly revenue shortfall comes to approximately Rs 13–14 crore.

This is a mix-based estimate, not management-confirmed lost revenue.

Q2 FY26 revenue was approximately Rs 199.8 crore, while Q2 FY27 revenue came in at Rs 206.3 crore. This translates into reported YoY growth of approximately 3.2%.

If we add back the estimated Rs 13–14 crore of deferred LATAM sales, normalised Q2 revenue would have been approximately Rs 219–220 crore.

That would imply YoY growth of approximately 10–11%, rather than the reported 3.2%.

So, our calculation suggests that the LATAM disruption could have reduced reported Q2 revenue growth by approximately 7 percentage points.

This is a meaningful difference when assessing the underlying business momentum.

One important clarification: these sales should not automatically be classified as permanently lost. Management's explanation is that some of the business is deferred pending customer authorizations. The actual recovery will depend on permits being granted and orders converting into shipments.

Also, this calculation assumes that the historical 20% LATAM contribution to exports is a reasonable normalised benchmark. It does not prove that every rupee of the estimated shortfall would have materialised.

What does this mean for the investment thesis?
I see two different aspects here.

First, the underlying business may have been growing faster than the reported Q2 numbers suggest. Our indicative calculation puts normalised Q2 growth closer to 10–11%, rather than 3.2%.

Second, the lost LATAM contribution has a disproportionate impact on profitability because these were higher-margin products.

Management itself attributed approximately 3 percentage points of EBITDA margin pressure to LATAM regulatory changes and product mix.

Therefore, even if revenue is replaced through semi-regulated markets, the same level of profitability may not immediately return.

This is why I would track revenue recovery and margin recovery separately.

What should we watch going forward?

I don't think there is any point in being overly smart at this stage or trying to predict exactly when everything will normalise. The next quarter will be important, and we should focus on actual evidence of recovery rather than management assurances.

The key things to monitor are whether customers in Colombia, Peru and Uruguay receive the required import authorizations, whether deferred LATAM orders convert into actual shipments, and whether the region's contribution starts moving back towards historical levels. I would also like management to provide greater clarity on the exact products affected, country-wise revenue exposure and the status of customer permits.

Alongside this, progress on new product launches, the CMO opportunity and Ambarnath ramp-up will determine the broader growth and margin recovery.

My overall view
There is a plausible regulatory explanation for the LATAM disruption, and historical sales trends suggest that this was an important, growing and higher-margin business for Supriya. However, we should not automatically assume that all deferred sales will return or that historical EBITDA margins will be restored.

For existing investors, the focus should be on whether the original investment thesis remains intact. For prospective investors, the opportunity needs to be evaluated against the uncertainty around revenue recovery, margins and execution.

I would rather wait for Q3 performance and actual evidence of recovery than make overly confident predictions based on management commentary alone.

Ultimately, we need to look at both sides: what was genuinely outside management's control and where communication, planning and execution could have been better. That is how we form an unbiased view of the business.

Note: Regulatory product overlaps mentioned above are based on publicly available lists and Supriya's published portfolio. They are not confirmation of the exact products affected in the company's LATAM orders. Revenue impact is our own indicative calculation, not a company-disclosed figure.

OnEMI Technology Solutions (KISSHT) | A Digital Lending Company I’m Quite Bullish On

A company that was managing ₹4,000 Cr worth of loans in March 2025 has now crossed ₹10,000 Cr!

And its quarterly profit has doubled in just one year🔥🔥🔥

I’ve been going through Kissht’s latest results and management concall. I think this is becoming a very interesting fintech growth story.

What exactly does Kissht do?

You might know Kissht as an instant personal loan app.

But the actual business is much bigger.

Through its NBFC subsidiary and lending partners, Kissht provides personal loans and loans against property.

What impressed me is its technology.

The company uses an AI-based underwriting system analysing more than 7,200 variables to assess borrowers.

It has already served over 1.28 crore customers and works with 45+ lending partners.

And here’s the interesting part.

Around 55% of its loan portfolio was managed through lending partners rather than sitting directly on its own balance sheet in September.

This partnership-led model allows Kissht to expand its lending business without funding every rupee of loans itself.

Now look at the financial numbers.

FY26:

Revenue: ₹2,179 Cr

PAT: ₹281 Cr (+75% YoY)

Q2FY27:

Total Income: ₹740 Cr (+43% YoY)

PAT: ₹125 Cr (+100% YoY)

AUM: ₹9,317 Cr (+68% YoY)

Quarterly Disbursements: ₹4,612 Cr (+56% YoY)

And on 4 November, the company announced that its AUM had already crossed ₹10,000 Cr.

But what caught my attention wasn’t just the growth.

Credit quality is actually improving alongside it.

Gross NPA has reduced to 2.18%.

Net NPA stands at just 0.34%.

Credit cost has declined from 9.3% to 6.2% of average AUM over the past year.

For a digital lending company growing this quickly, these numbers are worth paying attention to.

Management’s Future Outlook

This is where I became more interested.

Management has increased its FY27 AUM growth guidance from 40%+ to 60%+.

It is also targeting:

• More than 15% YoY reduction in credit cost

• Return on Equity above 20%

• Gross NPA below 2.25%

• Further reduction in borrowing costs

The company recently raised another ₹832 Cr through a preferential issue, strengthening its capital base for expansion.

Management believes it can scale substantially further without another equity fundraise.

My Future View

I’m bullish on Kissht’s business growth over the next 2–3 years.

The combination of digital customer acquisition, AI-based underwriting, improving credit costs and lower borrowing expenses could create meaningful earnings growth.

My aggressive FY28 scenario is a loan portfolio of ₹18,000–20,000 Cr with PAT potentially reaching ₹650 Cr.

These are my estimates, not management guidance.

At around ₹354, Kissht commands a market cap of roughly ₹7,200 Cr.

Based on approximately ₹379 Cr trailing annual profit, that works out to around 19× earnings.

For a lender growing this quickly while delivering over 20% ROE, I find that valuation interesting.

The biggest risk is that more than 90% of its loan portfolio is still unsecured. A deterioration in borrower repayments could change the earnings picture quickly.

But my view remains positive.

I believe Kissht has the potential to become a much larger, highly profitable digital lending business if it maintains its underwriting discipline.

The most interesting part isn’t how quickly Kissht can give someone a loan. It’s how quickly it can scale that business without letting bad loans catch up.

That’s the story I’ll be tracking closely.

Digi Lenders Clock 50% Revenue Growth as Credit Demand Surges: Kissht, Moneyview, MobiKwik and Paytm Report 41-49% Revenue Growth in September Quarter; Retail NBFC Lending Up 21.9% as Rising Indebtedness Sparks Caution

Core Theme 
Digital lenders are growing 41-49% as banks’ slower pace in unsecured credit leaves younger and self-employed borrowers to fintechs, with disbursements surging across Kissht, Moneyview and MobiKwik, though the faster rise in retail borrowing across the system is prompting caution about rising indebtedness.

The Growth: Fintech Scorecard
Listed new-age fintech companies reported 40-50% growth in lending and financial services revenue in the September quarter, driven by strong loan disbursements and rising demand for unsecured credit from younger borrowers

Kissht: revenue from operations rose 44.7% YoY to ₹732 crore; Q2 disbursals ₹4,612 crore; AUM ₹9,317 crore

Moneyview: revenue grew 41% to ₹1,120 crore; Q2 disbursals ₹7,701 crore; AUM ₹23,892 crore

MobiKwik: financial services revenue increased 41.8% to ₹87 crore; Q2 disbursals ₹1,083 crore

Paytm: financial services distribution revenue grew 49.3% to ₹912 crore (includes broking and wealth products; revenue metrics not directly comparable across companies)

Loan Disbursements: The Pace
Moneyview facilitated loans worth ₹7,701 crore in the quarter, up 41.3% YoY

Kissht’s disbursements rose 56% to ₹4,612 crore

MobiKwik reported a 34% increase to ₹1,083 crore

The figures include loans originated through lending partners as well as their own NBFC subsidiaries

Moneyview, which primarily serves consumers outside India’s largest cities, said about 75% of its lending capital comes from partner institutions, allowing it to expand without proportionally increasing its own balance sheet

Broader Credit Backdrop
The growth reflects a broader expansion in household and small-business credit, a key indicator of domestic consumption and economic activity

According to the RBI, retail lending by non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) grew 21.9% YoY in September, compared with 16.8% a year earlier

Banks’ personal loan portfolios expanded 17.3% during the same period, against 11.5% last year

Larger Lenders Also Benefiting
Bajaj Finance reported a 26% increase in AUM to ₹5.85 lakh crore, booking 13.45 million new loans, up 11%; quarterly disbursements jumped 47% to ₹35,872 crore

Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company’s AUM grew 25% to ₹2.68 lakh crore

Why Fintechs Are Winning
Jinay Gala, director at India Ratings & Research: the relatively smaller base of digital lenders and their ability to reach borrowers underserved by traditional financial institutions were driving faster growth

“Banks have been slow on personal loans and unsecured lending, allowing fintechs to serve more self-employed and Gen Z borrowers,” he said

ET Insight: by capturing the Gen Z wallet, digital platforms have positioned themselves as the primary gatekeepers of future retail consumption

While in Tier-1 cities, you can find dozens of good schools. But once you move to Tier-3/4 towns or villages, you might find only a handful of genuinely good schools.

Millions of families in India belong to the middle-class and below-middle-class segments. Some struggle to make ends meet every month, while others manage to move one step at a time, create opportunities and help their children succeed.

The same applies to listed companies. We have thousands of them, but many will disappear or fail over the next 7–10 years. A handful, however, will go on to become much bigger businesses.

What's the common characteristic here?

Maybe God's divine blessings or a bit of luck. But, more often than not, it comes down to hard work, discipline and managing things better.

One word that captures all these attributes is MANAGEMENT.

The headmaster/headmistress and a handful of dedicated teachers would have made all the difference to those few good schools. Similarly, disciplined, hardworking and financially conscious parents would have made the difference to those families and their children's futures.

We keep looking for good stock ideas. Perhaps we should change the starting point.

Look for good management teams with ethics, hunger, aspiration and a willingness to work hard. These are the businesses that have the potential to create consistent wealth for shareholders.

Laurus Labs, Sansera Engineering, Sona BLW, Innomet Advanced and OBSC Perfection are a few examples.

Listen to their concalls, follow their media interactions and observe their behavior. Look for signs of inconsistency, lack of discipline, excessive storytelling or capital misallocation. Equally importantly, look for evidence that management walks the talk.

When you don't find these red flags and continue to see evidence of execution, you know you have a business worth shortlisting.

Once we shortlist a company, at what valuation to buy and at what valuation to sell is a personal choice, driven by conviction and data.

But perhaps we should change the sequence. Start with management, hunger and aspiration. Don't start with valuations and PAT.

Happy Diwali!

Financial Year 2025-26 marked a structural turning point for Timex Group, ending as a milestone year that fundamentally transformed the company's scale and profitability profile. Total revenue surged 48% year-on-year to ₹800 crore.

The growth was driven by a decisive shift toward premiumization. The core Timex brand expanded 62%, fashion powerhouse Guess grew 51%, and luxury anchor Versace delivered 48% growth. At the same time, e-commerce and quick commerce channels recorded a phenomenal 90% increase, highlighting the strength of the company's omnichannel strategy.

More importantly, profitability significantly outpaced revenue growth as operating leverage began to play out.

What makes this performance particularly noteworthy is that it was not driven by a single exceptional quarter. Revenue growth remained consistently strong throughout the year, with Q1 growing 55% YoY, Q2 40%, Q3 26%, and Q4 an impressive 74% YoY.

The company's sales strategy appears to be creating a sustainable high-growth trajectory. Historically, Q2 has been the strongest quarter due to festive-season bookings, while the remaining quarters were relatively subdued. This year, however, Q4 revenue reached almost 96% of Q2 levels, indicating a far more balanced and resilient demand profile across the year.

What to Expect in FY27 and FY28?

Management is positioning the company to enter the ₹1,100-1200-crore revenue club, targeting a base-case growth rate of 35-40%. This expansion will be supported by a significant increase in local manufacturing capacity, which is expected to rise from 6 million units to 10 million units annually.

While the company continues to prioritize growth, EBITDA margins are expected to stabilize in the 15–16% range. Additionally, employee expenses and administrative overheads appear to have largely normalized, creating the potential for substantial operating leverage as revenues continue to scale.

Latest update (post Q2FY27):

Posted highest-ever quarterly revenue of ₹359 crores. E-commerce grew 75% in Q2, led by Flipkart, Myntra, Amazon, 3P and quick commerce.

The Baddi plant is operating at 100% capacity (6 million units/year) and ran double shifts to meet demand. Investing $1.2 million to double the Baddi plant's capacity to 12 million units by May of next year.

In the ₹2,000–10,000 segment, the competitive landscape is largely a duopoly between Titan and Timex. While Titan's core brand business is still nearly 4x the size of Timex, management sees significant headroom to capture market share and scale up.

The company sees a potential to reach an EBITDA margin of ~20% in the future through operating leverage.

Last but not least, festive season shopping fell in Q2 last year, whereas this year it has shifted to Q3. Hence, do expect some fireworks in Q3FY27!

3. Navin Fluorine

How they make money:

Navin earns its revenue from three verticals. The business operates across i) High Performance Products (refrigerants and inorganic fluorides) - 51%, ii) Specialty Chemicals (agrochemical and industrial intermediates) - 30%, and iii) CDMO (pharma synthesis) with emerging Advanced Materials - 19%.

HPP (High Performance Products) is the biggest and covers refrigerant gases (HFCs, R32 coming), AHF/HF sold to merchant and high-purity buyers, and the HFO supply contract with Solstice Advanced Materials (the old Honeywell/Orchid business), which is a pass-through-priced, long-tenure contract on a dedicated asset.

Specialty Chemicals is mostly agrochemical and fluorination intermediates made in the multi-purpose plants (MPP-1/MPP-2) at Dahej on a campaign basis. It is running at roughly a ₹350 cr per quarter run rate, and the Nectar/Chemours project is being added.

CDMO is largely Fermion/darolutamide, made in dedicated cGMP plants, with a USD100M target for FY27 and a pipeline of other molecules behind it. Advanced Materials (data centres, semiconductors, defence, the DRDO/TDF project) is being incubated as a fourth vertical, expected to be 10-15% of the pie by 2030.

What’s working well:

Q2 revenue was ₹1,191 cr (+57% YoY), EBITDA ₹407 cr (+66%) at a 34.2% margin, and PAT ₹269 cr (+81%). H1 PAT of ₹513 cr already gives an EPS of ₹100. All three segments grew sequentially.

HPP benefited from better refrigerant gas placement than the market average, the AHF plant ramping, and higher HFO volumes.

Specialty gained from squeezing more campaigns out of existing MPP plants, and CDMO from the Fermion base plus new qualification campaigns. Gross profit held despite input inflation because forex tailwinds, pricing actions, operating leverage and efficiency gains offset sourcing costs. Working capital is at 72 days, capex is funded comfortably (H1 capex was about ₹300 cr), and the Solstice HFO contract was extended from 7 to 11 years (to December 2032) with about USD180M of added revenue potential. This protects the base beyond FY28, though the implied ~USD45M/yr run rate versus the earlier ~USD58M drew few "ouch" comments. Management says the pass-through pricing makes simple averaging misleading and that volumes are guaranteed higher.

What to expect for the rest of FY27 and FY28:

Management guided FY27 margins to stay in the H1 range (~34%), while keeping the long-term 30% EBITDA guidance unchanged. Q3 and Q4 should add several visible steps. The MPP debottlenecking (commissioned end-September) is not yet in the numbers, and R32 should give incremental revenue in Q3 with a full ramp in Q4. The Chemours project is due in Q3 with orders already in hand, and cGMP-4 Phase 2 (~₹125 cr) should start by the end of Q4.

Specialty should reach about 60-65% of Nectar’s peak annual revenue in FY27, with the rest in FY28, and CDMO should reach the USD100M order-book target. FY27 capex is guided at about ₹700 cr, at the low end of the ₹700-1,000 cr annual frame. Management says FY28 growth is “pretty much baked in” from the capex already in place, so expect continued 20-25% type growth, with cGMP-4 (₹900-1,000 cr peak potential, split across Phase 1 and Phase 2) mostly a FY28-FY29 story.

Advanced Materials adoption capacity arrives by Q2 FY28. The main swing factors are geopolitics and input costs (fluorspar, sulphur and gas are all rising), the pace of AHF utilisation, how much of the current refrigerant pricing proves durable, and whether Chemours adoption (a ~15-month read after commissioning) justifies the larger scale-up.

4. Innomet Advanced

How they make money

Innomet is a Hyderabad-based maker of engineered metal products with two divisions.

i) Metal powders (about ₹38 cr in H1, roughly 68% of revenue) are specialty powders sold by weight to parts makers, additive manufacturing and surface-coating customers. Almost 100% of this is water-atomised, and gas-atomised spherical powder has only just started with a 50 kg unit. Realisation rose from ₹959 to ₹1,487/kg.

ii) Tungsten heavy alloys (THA) (₹17.6 cr, about a third of revenue) are dense, high-value parts and fragments for defence (Pinaka, Astra), aerospace (AS9100D-certified) and other niche uses, sold per piece or per kg (₹25,000-35,000/kg indicated), with about 87% exported. Tungsten feedstock is now partly captured through the 57.5% acquisition of Swastik Tungsten, which was consolidated only for the last few days of H1. Exports were 46% of H1 revenue, against 15% a year ago. Management gave segment EBITDA margins of about 12% for powders and about 22% for THA, which blend to the reported ~15%.

What’s working well

H1 revenue more than doubled to ₹55.7 cr (from ₹23.5 cr), already above all of FY26. EBITDA was ₹8.24 cr at a 14.8% margin, up from 4.4% in H2 FY26 when tungsten prices squeezed profits, though still below 18% a year ago. PAT was ₹4.75 cr and EPS ₹3.64. Powder volumes rose 39% with 55% higher realisation, and 18 new customers were added (including Oerlikon and Medicoat). THA grew about sixfold and its mix rose from 14% to a third, which should lift margins as it grows. Exports rose about sevenfold, helped by China-plus-one sourcing, defence restocking and aerospace certification, and powder sales to the US continue despite the 50% tariff. The tungsten supply problem is described as solved by Swastik, with sourcing vendors up from 2-3 to over 60. Pricing discipline has improved (buying only against confirmed orders, shorter quote validity), and the balance sheet looks fine, with debt-to-equity at 0.36x, net worth up to ₹55 cr, and ₹37.5 cr of preferential funding (about ₹14 cr received).

What to expect for the rest of FY27 and FY28

With ₹55.7 cr delivered and ₹36.7 cr of orders in hand, FY27 revenue should clear the ₹100 cr target, and management says H2 will be “much better” than H1 if all goes well. Tungsten prices have stabilised after a sharp rise, so deferred customer orders (Indian defence programmes and Israeli buyers still in test mode) may start flowing.

Powder capacity rises from 620 to 800 tpa this year, then to 1,350 tpa in FY28 and about 1,600 tpa with the DRDO-backed atomiser.

THA’s current output is about 60 tpa (2-2.5 tonnes a month), and the 120 tpa expansion could support about ₹150 cr of revenue at current prices. Management guides FY28 growth of 30-50% (35-50% for the next two to three years) with better margins, and a long-term EBITDA margin of 16-20%. Their view is that existing assets can reach ₹400-500 cr, while the ₹1,000 cr vision depends on a new greenfield project and fresh fundraising that is “not even on the drawing board”. Swastik’s bottom line won’t improve until it moves up to carbide and pure-tungsten products, at least six months away. Tungsten hexafluoride for semiconductors is a “moonshot”, and the spark plasma sintering furnace and the EIGA atomiser for reactive powders (titanium, zirconium) are early-stage.

But if the company has to achieve ₹1,000 Cr in revenue, Tungsten Carbide is perhaps the most realistic growth avenue to get there!

5. Indo Count Industries

How they make money

Indo Count is a bed-linen and home-textile maker that sells to large retailers, mainly in the US. It runs in two segments.

The core business is bed linen made in India (sheets, duvet covers and similar), with a FY27 revenue target of about ₹4,000 cr and EBITDA margins of roughly 15% or better. Core revenue is about 70% US and about 30% non-US.

The new businesses have a FY27 target of about ₹1,500 cr. They are split roughly two-thirds utility bedding and one-third branded. Utility bedding (quilts, comforters, blankets and similar) is made in three US facilities. The branded side is built around Wamsutta, a US brand the company acquired, plus licensed brands such as Tommy Hilfiger. Revenue comes from product sales: volumes in million meters multiplied by realisation, plus the margin from branded and utility products. 

Management said gross margin should be viewed on an annual basis and should stay in a 50–55% range. Cotton is the main input cost. The company holds 4–5 months of inventory as a cushion and passes cost increases on to customers with a lag of one to two quarters. Most sales are on FOB or CIF terms, so freight increases are borne by the customer.

What’s working well

Execution is strong across the business. Q2 total income was ₹1,699 cr (+57% YoY, +39% QoQ), and EBITDA more than doubled to ₹259 cr at a 15.3% margin, against a full-year guidance of 13%. H1 revenue of ₹2,923 cr is about 52% of the full-year target, and H1 EBITDA margin is 14.4%. Management attributed the growth to market-share and wallet-share gains. Core margins are above 15%. The new businesses have reached about 30% of revenue, with Q2 revenue of about ₹502 cr and about 60% of the FY27 target already done. The three US utility plants are running above 65% utilisation. Wamsutta’s move into US retail, beyond direct-to-consumer, is a big driver on the branded side. 

The balance sheet is at its best: net debt is ₹518 cr (0.2x equity, the lowest ever), cash is ₹315 cr, annualised ROCE is 21.4% and ROE is 15.3%. Management also said working-capital days are down by at least three weeks since March, and the pass-through mechanism has protected margins so far.

Two caveats: Q2 gross margin fell, and management put that down to product mix. The new businesses’ EBITDA margin is still only “lower double digit”.

What to expect for rest of FY27 and FY28

For FY27, management said it will exceed the ₹5,500 cr revenue guidance and the 13% EBITDA margin guidance. Volume guidance is 105–110 million meters, with 51 million done in H1. The margin could reach 14–15% for the year, but management said it will not go beyond that. Rough arithmetic from the H1 run-rate suggests revenue of about ₹6,000 cr or more, though management gave no number. The new businesses’ margins should rise from lower double digits toward the core’s 15% over the next two to three quarters as the US plants fill up. The ₹250 cr capex is spread over 12–18 months, with only about ₹40 cr spent in H1. Most of the spinning capex should land in FY27, and the effluent treatment plant will probably spill into FY28. For FY28, the stated goal is ₹8,000 cr of revenue by CY28 (double the FY25 base of ₹4,000 cr), and management said this needs no growth capex. Utility plants should reach full utilisation and the branded business should reach about $100 mn, both by CY28.

The UK FTA took effect in July and the EU deal is still pending, and non-US revenue should grow by more than 20% in FY27. Management will give FY28 guidance next year. Net debt should keep falling as free cash flow comes in.

The stock subsequently gained around 4.5% to ₹2,700 in the price data reviewed.

This is an interesting example of a large shareholder exit being absorbed by identifiable global institutional investors.

Investor watch: Used-car penetration, transaction volumes, growth, profitability and valuation.

4. GO FASHION: PROMOTER BUYING + PLEDGE RELEASE

The promoter group purchased approximately ₹24.8 crore worth of shares.
At the same time:

• Franklin MF sold approximately ₹32.7 crore.
• Promoter-related pledge release of approximately ₹41.7 crore was reported.
• The stock gained around 10.1% in the price data reviewed.

The combination of promoter buying and pledge release is worth monitoring.

However, it does not by itself establish a business turnaround.

Investor watch: Further promoter purchases, pledge levels and operating performance.

5. ALIVUS LIFE SCIENCES: SEVEN BUYERS ABSORB NIRMA'S EXIT

Nirma sold approximately ₹390 crore worth of shares.

The disclosed transaction data showed seven buyers absorbing the entire sale.

The stock subsequently gained around 8.1%.
A diversified buyer base can be constructive, but the identity and investment horizon of the buyers matter.

Investor watch: New shareholder profile, earnings growth, margins and valuation.

OTHER INSTITUTIONAL ACCUMULATION SIGNALS

A few more names deserve attention:

• Tata Steel: ICICI Group increased its holding by approximately 1.04 pp to 3.35%.

• AstraZeneca Pharma India: ICICI Group added approximately 0.79 pp to 2.18%.

• Punjab Chemicals: Ares Diversified increased its holding by approximately 1.46 pp to 4.89%.

• Ardee Industries: Ashish Kacholia crossed the 1% holding threshold, with a reported holding of 1.20%.

• Horizon Industrial Parks: Radhakishan Damani held 1.16%; SBI Group held 1.45%.

These are research leads, not automatic buy signals. The reporting period behind each shareholding change needs to be checked.

PROMOTER SELLING: WHO IS MONETISING?

Insider trading disclosures showed:

• Open-market purchases: approximately ₹206 crore
• Open-market sales: approximately ₹959 crore
• Sell-to-buy ratio: approximately 4.7 times by value

However, three names—Sri Lotus Developers, Shreeji Shipping and Dr Reddy's KMP—accounted for approximately 93% of the reported market-sale value.

Some notable transactions:

• Sri Lotus Developers: Promoter Anand Pandit sold approximately ₹573 crore, representing around 4.88% of equity. Promoter holding remained approximately 65%.

• V2 Retail: Promoters sold approximately ₹258 crore, representing around 4.4% of equity, to six private buyers.

• Gallantt Ispat: Promoter Dinesh Agarwal sold approximately ₹250.5 crore through a block deal, plus around ₹20 crore through market transactions.

• Shreeji Shipping Global: Promoters sold approximately 1.84% of equity, worth around ₹257 crore, through market transactions.

Promoter selling is not automatically negative. The important questions are:
How much equity is being sold?
What is the promoter's residual holding?
Who is absorbing the shares?
Is the selling recurring?

The identity of the buyer matters as much as the identity of the seller.

LARGE SHAREHOLDER EXITS: NOT ALL ABSORPTION IS EQUAL

Two transactions illustrate why investors should look beyond headline deal values.

LENSKART
SVF II Lightbulb exited approximately ₹1,846 crore worth of shares.
Disclosed buyers substantially matched the sale value. Kotak MF bought approximately ₹331 crore, while a significant portion was routed through Societe Generale, Goldman Sachs and BNP desks.

The stock gained around 4%.

Good absorption, but the ultimate end-clients behind the investment-bank desks remain partly undisclosed.

GROWW

Peak XV and YC Holdings sold approximately ₹2,457 crore worth of shares.

Goldman Sachs ODI was identified as a buyer of approximately ₹764 crore—around 31% of the sale.

The remaining ₹1,693 crore was not identifiable from the available disclosed buyer information.

This is a substantial exit, but the ultimate ownership of the balance remains unclear.

Key lesson: A transaction routed through an investment bank does not automatically represent long-term institutional buying.

PLEDGES: ONE LARGE DEVELOPMENT TO MONITOR
Knowledge Realty Trust reported pledge creation by four Blackstone sponsor entities.
• Approximately 60.7 crore units pledged.
• Equivalent to around 13.7% of the trust.
• Reported value: approximately ₹6,719 crore at ₹110.60 per unit.

The lender and purpose were not disclosed in the dataset.

Other developments:

• Swan Corp: approximately ₹280 crore pledge creation.
• Ravindra Energy: approximately ₹57.5 crore pledge creation.
• Go Fashion: approximately ₹41.7 crore pledge release.
• ideaForge: approximately ₹25 crore pledge release.
• Responsive Industries: approximately ₹14.5 crore pledge release.

A pledge does not automatically imply financial distress. But large sponsor-level pledges deserve scrutiny, particularly around the financing purpose, collateral terms and potential invocation risk.

STRATEGIC OWNERSHIP CHANGE: GRT JEWELLERS AND TBZ

GRT Jewellers acquired approximately 74.12% of Tribhovandas Bhimji Zaveri (TBZ) through an off-market transaction.

• Shares acquired: approximately 4.95 crore
• Transaction price: ₹209 per share
• Consideration: approximately ₹1,034 crore

This is a strategic change in ownership, not an ordinary block deal.

Investors should track the applicable open-offer requirements or exemptions, final offer terms, acquisition rationale and the potential for operating synergies.

6/8 🧪 Supriya Lifescience: Topline Holding, Bottomline Pressure

Revenue: ₹206.3 Cr (+3.2% YoY)

EBITDA: ₹45.4 Cr (Margin down to 22.0% vs 36.4% YoY)

Net Profit (PAT): ₹29.25 Cr (-42% YoY)

Commentary: Severely impacted by higher operating and expansion expenses. Positives include the launch of two new anaesthetic inhalation lines at Ambernath and an ongoing EU compliance audit. 

#supriyalifesciences

Supriya Lifescience... I was expecting much better from this company.

PAT down 42%, margins fallen from 36% to 22%.

But what surprised me more was the earnings call.

In August management was talking about 33–35% margins. Now suddenly 23–25%.

Ambernath plant is not contributing, LATAM business has regulatory issues and raw material costs have increased.

All these may be temporary problems. But how could management be so confident just 3 months back?

One good thing, cash flow is positive, receivables have come down and company has no bank debt. So there is time to correct things.

I still like its move towards specialty APIs and formulations.

But now I would watch actual orders and sales from Ambernath rather than another guidance.

And even after 20% fall, valuation is not very cheap.

Sometimes one bad quarter can be ignored. But when management's expectations change so sharply in just 3 months, I think we need to be more careful.

Sansera Engineering: Q2 FY27 Results and Key Takeaways from the Concall

Sansera had its highest ever quarterly revenue and EBITDA. Margins went up despite higher wages and freight costs. The aerospace, defence and semiconductor (ADS) order book jumped about 32% in one quarter.

Q2 FY27
Revenue: ₹1,091.5 Cr (+32% YoY)
EBITDA: ₹211.2 Cr (+48% YoY) | Margin 19.4% (+~200 bps)
PAT: ₹108.6 Cr (+52% YoY)
Gross margin: 43% (+180 bps)

H1 FY27
Revenue: ₹2,112.7 Cr (+33% YoY)
EBITDA: ₹407.3 Cr (+48% YoY) | Margin 19.3%
PAT: ₹196 Cr (+46% YoY)

ADS revenue: ₹164.3 Cr in Q2 | Non-auto share of sales: 20.9%

(YoY = Year on Year, EBITDA = Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation, PAT = Profit After Tax, ADS = Aerospace, Defence and Semiconductor, bps = basis points, where 100 bps = 1%)

Key Takeaways

1.  Diversification target nearly reached-
Engine-based (ICE, Internal Combustion Engine) auto parts are now about 65% of sales, close to the target Sansera set at its IPO. The ICE business itself grew 18% to ₹669.7 Cr, so the share is falling because the new segments are growing faster. EV and fuel-agnostic parts posted a record ₹136.3 Cr.

2.  ADS order book jumped-
The ADS order book rose to ₹5,870 Cr from ₹4,440 Cr in June. It includes a large semiconductor order and will be executed over 5 years. Sansera won its first order from Safran (French aircraft engine maker) and added new aerospace customers. A second semiconductor customer is expected in Q3.

3.  Capex raised to build capacity-
FY27 capex is raised from ₹500 Cr to ₹800 Cr, with about half going to ADS. Once all the planned ADS plants are running, they can support roughly ₹3,000-3,500 Cr of ADS revenue. Net debt rose to ₹261 Cr (still only 0.3x EBITDA), and interest cost went up to ₹14.6 Cr from ₹8.1 Cr.

4.  Costs are rising-
Karnataka raised minimum wages by about 30%, and Sansera booked a ₹16.7 Cr provision this quarter. This is a recurring cost. The West Asia conflict also pushed up the cost of cutting tools, freight and logistics. A better product mix and higher volumes helped absorb these costs.

5.  New growth options-
The Nichidai JV (Joint Venture) will make steering and driveline forgings, with production starting by end of FY27. Sansera is developing complex parts for a North American humanoid robot maker. It also expects validation in Q3 on a jet engine part (blisk) under development for a global engine maker.

6.  Auto order book is healthy-
The non-ADS order book (measured as peak annual sales) rose to ₹2,240 Cr from ₹1,850 Cr, and about half of it is for exports. Sansera got a pilot order from a two-wheeler company that is starting to outsource parts. The plan for a US plant is on hold because of tariff uncertainty.

Key Guidance
• FY27 revenue of ₹4,250-4,300 Cr
• ADS to grow from ~15% to 35-40% of revenue by FY31
• A new 5-year vision with fresh targets to be announced by end of FY27

🚨 US DATA CENTER RESTRICTIONS: WHAT IT MEANS FOR AI INFRASTRUCTURE STOCKS

Goldman Sachs estimates that nearly 45% of planned US data center capacity is located in states where new construction restrictions could emerge following recent election developments.

⚠️ Important: This does NOT mean 45% of data centers are cancelled. Projects may face approval delays, higher costs or relocation.

Why are restrictions being discussed?
• Rising electricity demand and power bills
• Water consumption and cooling requirements
• Pressure on local power grids
• Environmental and community concerns

Potential impact on Indian companies:

🔹 HFCL: Optical fibre, telecom networks and data center connectivity.

🔹 Sterlite Technologies (STL): Strong exposure to US AI data center optical connectivity, including a multi-year product award exceeding $1 billion.

🔹 Black Box: Data center infrastructure, system integration, networking and digital infrastructure solutions.

🔹 Aeroflex Industries: Supplies flexible flow solutions used in industrial and infrastructure applications. Its direct exposure to US AI data centers is different from optical fibre and connectivity companies.

What about Indian Data Centers? 🇮🇳

India’s data center expansion is driven by domestic cloud demand, AI adoption, digitalisation and investments by global technology companies.

US construction restrictions do not automatically affect Indian data center projects. However, global supply chains, equipment costs, financing and technology investments could influence the sector.

My Investment View:

Delayed projects do not necessarily mean lost demand.
Orders and deliveries could shift to later quarters.
Projects may move to states or countries with fewer restrictions.
Permanent cancellations would be a more serious concern.
Investors should monitor order execution, revenue growth, margins and cash flows rather than focusing only on order book numbers.

KEY TAKEAWAY:

AI infrastructure demand remains a long-term opportunity, but execution timelines and project approvals are becoming increasingly important.

Don’t confuse temporary delays with the end of the AI infrastructure boom. Also, don’t assume every company will benefit equally.

Supriya Lifescience: Q2 FY27 Results and Key Takeaways from the Concall

This was a weak quarter. Revenue was almost flat and EBITDA fell sharply, and management cut its margin guidance only one quarter after reaffirming it.

Q2 FY27
Revenue: ₹206 Cr (+3.2% YoY)
EBITDA: ₹45 Cr (-38% YoY) | Margin 22% (vs ~36% last year)
PAT margin: 14.2%

H1 FY27
Revenue: ₹396 Cr (+14.8% YoY)
EBITDA: ₹93 Cr (-25% YoY) | Margin 23.4%
PAT: ₹53 Cr (vs ₹85 Cr)

(YoY = Year on Year, EBITDA = Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortisation, PAT = Profit After Tax, API = Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient, the main chemical in a medicine)

Key Takeaways

1.  Where the margin went-
Supriya normally earns 34-35% EBITDA margin, and this quarter it fell to 22%. Management broke down the gap. About 6% came from costs at the new Ambarnath plant, which has no revenue yet. About 3% came from losing high-margin sales in Latin America, and about 3% from higher raw material and solvent prices.

2.  Latin America rule change-
Colombia, Peru and Uruguay have suddenly classified some of Supriya's high-margin products as "controlled substances". Customers there now need import permits, which take 4-5 months. Latin America's share of revenue fell from 21% to 12%. Management says demand has been delayed, not lost.

3.  Ambarnath is a cost for now-
The Ambarnath plant will cost about ₹60 Cr this year with almost no revenue, because the EU (European Union) inspection got delayed. The audit is happening this month. Management says the plant breaks even at ₹160-200 Cr revenue, which could take 1-1.5 years after approval. Its full potential is ₹450-500 Cr.

4.  New products and a big contract-
Two new anaesthetic products have been launched, and a US approval for one of them is expected soon. A large CMO (Contract Manufacturing Organisation) deal for this anaesthetic is "very close to signing". It will start with API supply, and the plant capacity for it is already built. Two ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder) drugs and a heart-drug intermediate are also scaling up.

5.  Revenue target looks stretched-
Management still targets ₹1,000 Cr revenue in FY27. H1 was ₹396 Cr, so H2 needs about ₹600 Cr, which is 1.5x the first half. Management pointed to ~₹265 Cr of inventory and firm orders. However, much of this growth is coming from semi-regulated markets where prices are lower.

6.  Investors questioned management communication-
On the Q1 call, management had said it was confident of 32-35% margins for the year. Several investors on this call said the sharp cut came without warning. Management said the Latin America rule change came after the Q1 call, and accepted the feedback. Investors should treat future guidance with some caution.

Key Guidance
• FY27 revenue of ₹1,000 Cr
• FY27 EBITDA margin cut to 23-25% (from 32-35% earlier); no FY28 margin guidance yet
• 20%+ revenue growth over the next 3-4 years
